newsitem.title: UK: Sainsbury hopes bank will enhance loyalty.
newsitem.headline: Sainsbury hopes bank will enhance loyalty.

text.p: British supermarket J. Sainsbury hopes that its new joint venture with Bank of Scotland, Sainsbury's Bank, will enhance customer loyalty and give an added marketing thrust to its brand, company spokesman Dominic Fry said.
"There should be significantly enhanced loyalty and we hope an additional marketing thrust," he said.
Sainsbury's Bank was launched on Wednesday with an Instant Access account which pays 5.75 percent gross annual interest and credit cards that can be used at Visa outlets.
Customers transferring balances to Sainsbury's Bank credit cards will receive incentives either in cash or in the Reward points that shoppers accumulate to receive goods or services.
Sainsbury, which holds 55 percent of the bank, does not expect to see any cost from the extra loyalty points offered.
Fry said the cost of the Reward points offered as incentives for customers would be carried by the bank, in which Bank of Scotland holds 45 percent.

Fry declined to be drawn on any forecasts for impact on sales of the banking offer, but said that current supermarket sales were "good," and that the supermarket's offer of extra Reward points on specified products since November "has been a big positive for us".
Fry said infrastructure charges for the bank, which will use telephone banking, were minimal, allowing it to offer "extremely competitive" interest rates.
The bank's credit cards will also offer customers Reward points for transactions at other stores, effectively allowing shoppers to gather Sainsbury loyalty points for purchases made at rival Tesco.
Sainsbury is the first of the supermarkets to launch a bank although Tesco has linked up with Royal Bank of Scotland and Safeway with Abbey National to provide financial services to customers.
